title: Parents sue school over 'inhumane' calming rooms after BBC report
description: Parents are suing a special school after a BBC investigation uncovered CCTV footage showing autistic children being locked inside calming rooms and ab
body: Parents are suing a special school after a BBC investigation uncovered CCTV footage showing autistic children being locked inside calming rooms and abused.Ten families are claiming that their children – all of whom had learning disabilities or several mental disorders - were amongst those harmed by their treatment in the rooms.A police investigation into the abuse, recorded inside the rooms at Whitefield special school in north London, ended two years ago without any charges.The school is now run by a new trust which says the failings have led to "important learning".Many special schools use seclusion spaces such as calming rooms outside of classrooms to address sensory needs or challenging behaviour.But the leaked footage obtained by the BBC showed children being shoved into padded rooms, thrown to the floor, restrained by the neck - or left alone, sitting in vomit.One 12-year-old boy appeared in over 55 hours of CCTV footage filmed inside the rooms.At the time, the Children's Commissioner for England, Dame Rachel de Souza, said the use of the rooms was "horrifying".Leigh Day is now bringing a civil legal claim on behalf of 10 families against the trust which ran the school and the London borough of Waltham Forest.The law firm says the use of the rooms was "barbaric", according to its clients. The claim alleges that children were falsely imprisoned and their human rights were breached."What was done to these children was profoundly harmful, and its impact continues to be felt by families every day", says Alison Millar, who is leading the case.The CCTV obtained by the BBC had been recorded between 2014 and 2017 but only emerged in 2021.Last month, a long-delayed review commissioned by Waltham Forest found that restraint and seclusion became "normalised" and a culture developed that allowed "pejorative views of non-compliant children".It added that parents were clear that the practices were "unimaginable" and "inhumane".The BBC has also found evidence of mistreatment in seclusion rooms at other schools across the UK.CCTV from a different school showed a boy being "brutally" and "unlawfully" restrained, while elsewhere an autistic child was kept inside a cage.The Department for Education has repeatedly declined to be interviewed about the failings in school seclusion rooms – or consider making CCTV installation mandatory inside them, as with nurseries.It did introduce a legal duty to record and report the use of seclusion.But the families of Whitefield children say this is not nearly enough – and would not prevent similar abuse happening again.The BBC also uncovered documents showing staff did record the use of seclusion for some pupils at Whitefield.One observation report of David Gloria's three-hour placement in a calming room recorded him crying on 38 separate occasions over the period, while asking to leave throughout.He was also documented saying he was "confused" and did not "understand" why he was there.David's father, Ricardo, said that nothing has changed that would prevent the abuse at Whitefield happening again and families have been abandoned to care for their traumatised children."The extended delays have hindered justice for the children who suffered unfair treatment at Whitefield's School over the years."It is crucial that some form of justice and a rehabilitation plan are established for the victims and their families."The Department for Education must act now to ensure the abuse at Whitefield never happens again, according to Jacqui Shurlock, chief executive of the charity  Challenging Behaviour Foundation."The DfE has not taken sufficient action to stop the use of rooms which sound therapeutic, but are in fact used to seclude children for lengthy periods, leading to significant harm."The Department for Education said it had also revised guidance on the use of seclusion and planned to respond to the council's safeguarding review."What happened at Whitefield was horrific, and a serious failure to protect children who needed it most", said a spokesperson.A spokesperson for Flourish Learning Trust, which ran the school when the footage was discovered, said it no longer operates any schools and none of the prior leadership are still in post."Whitefield School itself is now being run by a different trust which supports the outcomes from the review and has been working hard to transform the school and give every pupil the care, dignity and support they rightfully deserve."A Waltham Forest spokesperson said: "We are aware of the civil legal action led by Leigh Day. We will not be commenting further while legal action is ongoing."

schema.headline: Parents sue school over 'inhumane' calming rooms after BBC report

title: Body of US climber Mallory Geis found after Broad Peak avalanche
description: The remains of US climber Mallory Geis have been found by rescuers following an avalanche on one of the world's highest mountains, a local government
body: The remains of US climber Mallory Geis have been found by rescuers following an avalanche on one of the world's highest mountains, a local government body says.Geis was part of a 10-person expedition that was on Pakistan's Broad Peak, on the border with China, when the avalanche happened on Thursday.According to US media, Geis was 39 and from the Texas city of San Antonio.Two other bodies – of Nadhira Ahmed Abdullah Al Harthy from Oman and Pur Bahadur Gurun from Nepal - have also been identified.All have been taken to a hospital by helicopter for "legal formalities regarding identification", according to the Information Department of Gilgit Baltistan, the local region. The Alpine Club of Pakistan initially said four bodies had been located on Pakistan's Broad Peak, before clarifying they had in fact found two bodies and a body part. Several others were spotted by aerial drones, it said, though their condition would not become clear until rescue efforts resume on Saturday and a search group can reach the area, which could take several hours. Bad weather has been hampering them.The Alpine Club of Pakistan added that the location of one climber remains unknown.The announcement that Geis' remains had been found came later on Friday.A search and rescue operation for the team began after reports an avalanche on Thursday on the 8,047-metre (26,400ft) peak in the Karakoram range.The multinational climbing group was being led by renowned Nepal-born climber Nirmal Purja, the Alpine Club of Pakistan said.He is known for climbing all 14 of the world's 8,000-metre-plus mountains in just over six months in 2019.The Alpine Club of Pakistan told the BBC it had seen movement from the GPS trackers of three members of the expedition, including Purja, but that a helicopter was unable to see anything at those locations.Rescuers later found one of the trackers smashed, leading them to believe that the movement they had seen may have been a glitch.The Alpine Club of Pakistan's communications lead Naila Kiani said the chances of survival in such harsh conditions after more than 24 hours were "very slim", but added that "miracles do happen".Earlier on Friday, the Alpine Club confirmed that two rescue helicopters had been sent by the Pakistan army, carrying rescue personnel and additional specialised equipment to support the rescue operation."The club prays for the safety and successful rescue of all the climbers and stands in solidarity with their families and the international mountaineering community during this difficult time," it said.Purja joined the British Army in 2003 and joined the Special Boat Service - the special forces unit of the Royal Navy - in 2009.He went to Everest Base Camp in 2012, and instead of returning to Kathmandu, he summitted the 6,119m Lobuche East mountain in Nepal - his first peak.Climbing alongside Purja was American Mallory Geis. In mid-June, she had posted on social media that she had new boots ready for what she called "her first big kid climbing expedition in Pakistan".She is tagged in a post from a travel company, Moving Mountains. The post says that Mallory would be with Pakistani national Sohail Sakhi and that it was her first attempt to climb Broad Peak.It was Sakhi's tracker that was found smashed, and he is the one team member who has not yet been spotted.Besides Purja, Sakhi and Geis, there are a few other significant names among the missing climbers, including Pur Bahadur Gurung - also known as Yukta - and Kili Pemba Sherpa.Yukta is certified by the International Federation of Mountain Guides Associations and is very close to completing the 14 peaks challenge, in which climbers attempt to climb the world's 14 mountains that rise at least 8,000m above sea level.Kili Pemba has so far summited Everest 15 times. In 2021, he was a member of a historic K2 winter expedition, along with several Nepali climbers including Purja.Pemba is also the guide who led double amputee Xia Boyu to summit Everest in 2018. Xia, a Chinese climber, lost both legs decades earlier while attempting to reach Everest's summit.Broad Peak is regarded as one of the more challenging mountains for expeditions and is ranked as the world's 12th highest peak.The first successful ascent of Broad Peak was in 1957, when a four-member Austrian expedition reached the summit.Since then, many more have climbed peak - and dozens have lost their lives on the mountain.One of Broad Peak's deadliest years was 2013, when at least six fatalities were recorded.Correction 31/7/26: A previous version of this story stated that four members of the expedition had been found dead, citing the Alpine Club of Pakistan. This was a miscommunication on its part and has since been amended.

schema.headline: Body of US climber Mallory Geis found after Broad Peak avalanche

title: Labour's Bev Craig elected new mayor of Greater Manchester
description: In the first round, Craig secured 47% of the vote, compared with Astley's 21%.This meant the ballot papers from voters who did not select either of th
body: In the first round, Craig secured 47% of the vote, compared with Astley's 21%.This meant the ballot papers from voters who did not select either of them as their first choice were brought back into play.They were checked to see if the second-preference votes were for either the Labour or Reform candidate.They were then added to the first-preference votes.Craig expanded her already significant lead.More than two million people across Greater Manchester's 10 boroughs were eligible to vote in the contest but turnout was just under 25%.Analysis of the votes showed that Craig came top of the poll in the first round of voting in all the 10 local authority areas that make up Greater Manchester.Astley came second in eight of the 10 areas, while the Green candidate Geraldine Coggins came second in Manchester and the Conservative candidate Phil Eckersley was second in Trafford.In her speech, Craig said: "For too many people across our region, life is simply too hard. The generational belief that we had, that if you work hard and do the right thing, your life will be better and the life of the community will be better, is something that many people just don't feel at the minute."She continued: "Everyone deserves a quality home in a good neighbourhood," said Craig, adding that people should be able to plan for their future and for that of their children.She added: "We have to move away from divisive politics, and we'll do it together."Congratulations came from Labour's deputy leader Lucy Powell, the MP for Manchester Central, who posted on X, external: "Huge congratulations to @bevcraig our fantastic new Mayor of Greater Manchester."Thank you to our tireless activists who have worked so hard to help deliver this win."

schema.headline: Labour's Bev Craig elected new mayor of Greater Manchester

title: Newcastle United: Eddie Howe steps down as head coach
description: Howe added: "After nearly five years of giving my life, heart and soul into the club with unrelenting energy, I feel that it is in the best interests
body: Howe added: "After nearly five years of giving my life, heart and soul into the club with unrelenting energy, I feel that it is in the best interests of both myself and the club to step away, recharge and take a break."Although it's been incredibly difficult to make this decision, I know in my heart that it's the right one."It has been the privilege of my lifetime to have been the manager of Newcastle United."Howe's coaches Jason Tindall, Graeme Jones, Stephen Purches and Simon Weatherstone will also leave St James' Park, as well as head of performance Dan Hodges.Howe took charge in November 2021 and steered the Magpies to an 11th-place finish that season.In 2022-23 they qualified for the Champions League and did so again in 2024-25, as well as winning the League Cup.Last season they reached the Champions League knockout phase for the first time, losing to Barcelona in the last 16, but lost 17 of their 38 Premier League games and failed to secure European football next season. "There have been so many incredible moments in our time here," Howe added. "From fighting relegation in our first season to the numerous unforgettable nights at St James' Park in the Champions League soon after. The progression was fast."Everyone came together, united and what a force we became. These are all memories that I will cherish for the rest of my life."Howe's final match in charge was a 4-1 defeat by Bristol City at Ashton Gate in a pre-season friendly on Wednesday.The Magpies have lost two key midfielders this summer - Sandro Tonali to Tottenham and Anthony Gordon to Barcelona, while Arsenal are chasing captain Bruno Guimaraes, who has made it clear he wants to join the Premier League champions. Last summer, Newcastle spent in the region of £240m on new players, but Howe was left frustrated when Alexander Isak's drawn-out transfer saga ended with the Sweden striker joining Liverpool for a British record of £125m. "I remain incredibly positive and enthusiastic about the future of Newcastle," said Howe."The club is in fantastic hands with a great leadership team and I have no doubt together, alongside whoever comes in to replace me, they will continue to deliver success on the pitch."Newcastle's chief executive David Hopkinson added: "Eddie and his staff leave with the deep gratitude and respect of everyone at Newcastle United, and with a lasting place in the club's history."While we are naturally disappointed to see Eddie leave, we remain immensely thankful for everything he has done for the club."

schema.headline: Newcastle United: Eddie Howe steps down as head coach

title: Ex-catering workers claim they are owed thousands in unpaid wages
description: Chrissy Bell is a senior advisor with Acas and spent 10 years working on its helpline. Acas provides free, impartial advice to employees and employers
body: Chrissy Bell is a senior advisor with Acas and spent 10 years working on its helpline. Acas provides free, impartial advice to employees and employers on workplace rights and disputes.  "If someone is expecting their wages on a certain date and it doesn't arrive or it doesn't arrive in full, then if people haven't got savings, even a small amount of difference can be the difference between them paying their bills and not being able to pay them," says Chrissy. She has this advice to anyone who believes they have not been paid the correct amount,"Firstly, work out the amount you should have been paid. So check payslips, timesheets, contracts and the first step is to speak to the employers, as there may have been a genuine mistake."If this does not work, she suggests putting a more formal grievance in writing, setting out any evidence, including timesheets, and then giving the employer a reasonable chance to respond.Finally, she says if it is not resolved internally after a reasonable amount of time then the person should consider making a claim to an employment tribunal if they are owed outstanding wages."If someone gets an award at an employment tribunal then there are systems in place to help them enforce it if necessary," she says. Martha Lindeque declined to provide a statement, but the BBC understands that her position is that she strongly denies the allegations made by her ex-staff.

schema.headline: Ex-catering workers claim they are owed thousands in unpaid wages

title: He bought a fitness supplement online to bulk up, but ended up losing his mind
description: Daniel Murphy thought he was taking a safe and tested dietary supplement that would help him put on muscle in the gym.But over the following two years
body: Daniel Murphy thought he was taking a safe and tested dietary supplement that would help him put on muscle in the gym.But over the following two years, his mental health spiralled to such a degree he ended up in a state of psychosis in which he believed his wife was trying to steal his business and his mother-in-law was going to kill him.Unknown to Daniel, the daily pills he had been taking had been mixed with testosterone.The 32-year-old is one of 54,000 consumers listed in a case against a multimillion-pound peptide company based in the US, which sold its products around the world.The owner of Paradigm Peptides, Matthew Kawa, was jailed for five years and 10 months on Thursday after he admitted deliberately selling unapproved medicines, trying to deceive people about what they were and illegally bringing the products into the country. His sister, Jennifer Stechkober, who also pleaded guilty to selling unapproved medicines, was sent to prison for a year and four months.Both admitted they had lied about where the pills were sourced, their purity and their company's testing procedures. Despite claiming the supplements were manufactured in the US, they were actually imported from China, India and several other countries. The pair also faked certificates of analysis, the documents that prove the safety and quality of a product.Paradigm Peptides' website had stated it "stringently" tested all their products to ensure "efficacy, purity and potency", but the pair admitted not testing or analysing any of the products they sold, so they had not been aware they had been mixed with testosterone.Testosterone is a steroid hormone, which the body naturally produces. It drives physical development, builds muscle, and controls sex drive, primarily in males, but it also supports health in females. There is a synthetic version which doctors can prescribe, but which can cause liver damage, serious psychiatric effects and heart and respiratory problems if taken without medical oversight. It can also cause infertility in men and increase the risk of testicular cancer.The Paradigm Peptides case is the biggest to rock the industry, an unregulated market which has exploded into the mainstream over the past 18 months.Peptides are short chains of amino acids that our bodies produce and have long been used to treat medical conditions, including diabetes. More recently, they are being used in weight-loss drugs - GLP-1s. Another type of drug sold by Paradigm Peptides was SARMs - Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators - which target specific tissues to increase muscle and bone mass.Both these types of unregulated injectable drugs have become increasingly popular in the online wellness community - including among many young influencers.Social media is inundated with people extolling the virtues of various substances - such as BPC-157, GHK-CU and TB 500 - all of which purport to help build muscle mass, help with tissue recovery, or improve skin health. They are not licensed, can only be sold for testing purposes and are not suitable for human consumption.Three years ago, Murphy says he was in a good place. He was married to Laura, and they had built a "very stable, consistent, beautiful life" in the Smoky mountains in Knoxville, Tennessee.Murphy had lost 130 pounds (59kg) and had "completed a major health transformation" through diet and exercise."I wasn't into gym culture - I wasn't a big gym bro or anything," he explains. "But after I had lost all that weight, I wanted to start building muscle and these supplements seemed like a safe way of doing that."Murphy thought he was taking a daily dose of SARMs. Like peptides, they are not approved for human use and are seen as experimental drugs with a risk of serious liver damage, thrombosis and heart problems.Murphy says he felt safe taking them because they were clearly labelled a "dietary supplement" and Paradigm claimed it had a contract with the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on various blogs, but this was not true."Like other victims, I trusted that the products were safe," he says. "They presented everything as research backed with claims of 99% purity - it was all a lie."Murphy started taking Paradigm's SARMs in January 2023. During the first few months, he says they seemed to be having a positive effect: he was able to do longer workouts and had more energy. Encouraged by fake research articles he had read on Paradigm Peptides's website, he then started taking other products too.Insomnia and mania began to set in - and that triggered him, he says, to "burn down" everything he had built - his marriage, his friendships, and his business.During the court proceedings, consultant psychiatrist and pharmacologist, Dr Erik Messamore, gave evidence to confirm that he believed Murphy had been suffering from a steroid-induced psychosis.As Murphy's life spun out of control, unknown to him, the FDA was already investigating Paradigm Peptides. It had been sending warning letters to the company since 2020 telling it to stop selling unapproved drugs. By September 2023, the FDA had seized SARMs products from Paradigm to carry out tests on them. It turned out, all the supplements had been mixed with testosterone.But it would take another six months before the FDA closed the business down.In the UK, Adam Taylor, professor of anatomy at Lancaster University, has been watching cases like this closely, as the scientific community continues to raise the alarm on this market which operates in a legal and regulatory middle zone. The products are not illegal to buy or own, but they are not approved for human use and so are not subject to the quality controls that govern pharmaceutical manufacturing."This might have happened in the US," Taylor says. "But consumers are at risk here in the UK, this is a global industry."He says a case like this demonstrates the magnitude of the risk, when "people think they are taking one product but it's actually something completely different"."So, they may also be getting additional side effects or different results that they can't explain."Murphy's wife Laura says her husband changed overnight. He had gone from a "loving partner" to a man who believed that she was "plotting" to take over his successful consulting business."One minute he would be crying and asking what was wrong with him, the next he would talk about wanting to take over Los Angeles," she says. "We had no history of mental illness in our family, Dan was so calm and stable before this happened."We did not know what to do."Life began to unravel. Murphy had an affair, was drinking copious amounts of alcohol, and felt his friends and family were out to get him - he even thought his mother-in-law wanted to murder him."I was in a full-blown psychosis - I believed that my loved ones were trying to hurt me and kill me," he recalls. "At this point, I've lost the plot. I'm not able to make any connection to the supplements, to anything that's happening."Then in December 2024, Murphy ran out of his supply of Paradigm Peptides supplements. It was then, he says, he felt his condition began to improve.Murphy and his family had no idea the FDA had been investigating the company, and it was not until February 2025 that he was told that the drugs he had been taking had been mixed with steroids."If only I had known, if the FDA had been more public, or even just put a notice on the Paradigm Peptides website. But instead, I'm taking this product and they know it's been cut with steroids," he says.So far, he says he seems to have made a full recovery. He is one of 167 of the victims who have come forward and sought a total of $78,317 (£58,169) compensation for the damage caused. Others had suffered blood clots, heart issues, anxiety and depression, the Department of Justice confirmed.Murphy says he realises now he was playing "Russian roulette" with his health and no longer takes supplements."Never again," he says, "and I'm speaking out now because I don't want people falling into the trap I fell into - that all supplements are safe. "I was gambling my health, my family and, in many respects, my life."

schema.headline: He bought a fitness supplement online to bulk up, but ended up losing his mind

title: Mykhailo Mudryk ban: Chelsea winger free to return to football after doping case resolved
description: The FA never previously disclosed details of the case, because their anti-doping programme is deemed strictly confidential.However, their statement on
body: The FA never previously disclosed details of the case, because their anti-doping programme is deemed strictly confidential.However, their statement on Friday confirmed Mudryk returned an adverse finding for meldonium, which can increase respiratory capacity and stamina, in an out-of-competition test on international duty with Ukraine in October 2024.He was charged by the FA in June 2025 and given a four-year suspension in January, which came to light in April after he appealed against the ban to Cas.The FA said the test showed "a low concentration" of the prohibited cardiovascular medication.It added that changes have since been made to the World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada) technical document regarding meldonium.The FA said the changes are "not retroactive" but noted that had Mudryk's test been conducted today then "the concentration of meldonium in the sample would not have been reported" and no adverse finding would have been recorded.In a separate case resolution agreement to his Cas appeal, Mudryk and the FA have now, with the agreement of Wada, resolved the proceedings, leaving him able to return to all forms of competition.Sources close to Mudryk say he is confident of returning to his best form, citing the work he has put in to maintain his fitness during 20 months on the sidelines.They also point to the support Chelsea have provided throughout the process, while adhering to the restrictions imposed by his suspension and respecting the legal proceedings.The Ukrainian received backing from the club from afar, while also being given the space to navigate what those close to him describe as an extremely difficult period.Under the terms of the suspension, Mudryk was unable to access Chelsea's training ground or work with club staff. His only known public interaction with members of the first-team squad came at the Conference League final celebrations in May 2025.To maintain his fitness, Mudryk paid for private coaching and hired goalkeepers for individual sessions while using a pitch at non-league club Uxbridge FC in London. He also organised a training camp in Austria, with videos from those sessions showing him scoring goals and taking part in attacking drills.However, those close to Mudryk acknowledge there is no substitute for training and competing alongside elite players on a daily basis. Mudryk is understood to be realistic about the challenge ahead, but believes he can overcome it.Chelsea are prepared to provide a pathway back into professional football. Whether that involves reintegration into the first team, a loan move - potentially involving sister club Strasbourg - or a permanent transfer remains to be seen.Whatever the outcome, the resolution of the case represents a significant moment for Mudryk. He now has the opportunity to resume his career and determine what the next chapter looks like.Having joined Chelsea in one of the most closely watched transfer sagas of 2023, his story at Stamford Bridge is not over yet.

schema.headline: Mykhailo Mudryk ban: Chelsea winger free to return to football after doping case resolved

title: How Sam Fender and Olivia Dean's Rein Me In broke the UK's singles chart record
description: This reworking of Rein Me In, from Fender's third studio album, the Mercury Prize-winning People Watching, features an extra verse about the breakdown
body: This reworking of Rein Me In, from Fender's third studio album, the Mercury Prize-winning People Watching, features an extra verse about the breakdown of a relationship from a female perspective, from Dean."[It's] very personal and reminded us of home, but when Olivia put her touch on it, it became a much more universal track," he told Radio 1, adding "that's what made it so huge and so beautiful".He said he wanted to "personally thank" Dean, who helped him achieve his first ever number one single, adding: "It wouldn't have happened without Olivia obviously, but now I feel like it belongs to the fans, they've made it what it is".When asked how he'd be celebrating the achievement, Fender joked "I think I'm just gonna have a really big sandwich".It hasn't been a straightforward ascent to the top for Rein Me In - originally released as a solo Fender track and repurposed as a duet in June 2025, it took eight months to reach number one in February this year.Dean said when the track came out, external that the original version of Rein Me In was her "favourite song on Sam's album" and  it was "a pleasure to write a new verse from a female perspective".A lot of the song's success as a duet comes from its authenticity, with the lyrics exploring the fallout from the end of a relationship and the difficulties faced by both parties as they try to move on from each other.Whilst Fender's verses feel full of anger and regret at not being able to open up and be the partner he wanted to be, they are complimented by the softer and more reflective tone of Dean's, in which she encourages him to try again to make it work.It has been described by Blunt Magazine's Jake Fitzpatrick, external as "stormy, tender and anthemic" and a "love letter to the kind of songwriting that knows when to burn slow".The song has also received praise amongst many critics and bloggers, including Cult Following's Ewan Gleadow, external, who says that Dean's addition helps it to find "a new depth", noting "charm is a big part of it too, with all those reflections on where you come from and where you're headed".Ben Mortimer, who runs Fender's label Polydor, described it as a "historic achievement" from "two homegrown stars" - Newcastle's Fender and London's Dean.In an interview with Radio 1 when the track first hit number one, Fender acknowledged the track's slow climb to the top, thanking "the internet".He also says he found it interesting that the track "travelled online and people came to it later, which is wonderful really because it's the music that's doing the talking".The song has become a mainstay on TikTok - a quick scroll through the social media app shows its use on everything from grand declarations of love to montages of holidays and even compilations of football goals and celebrations.It's also notable that the song first went viral after the pair performed it at a show at the London Stadium, home of Dean's team West Ham, in June last year.She then returned the favour a week later at Newcastle United's St James Park, performing the song this time at the home of Fender's footballing love.Whilst TikTok streams do not count towards the official charts, BBC research from last year explored how much of an effect the platform was having on what we listened to, particularly songs with meaningful and powerful lyrics.

schema.headline: How Sam Fender and Olivia Dean's Rein Me In broke the UK's singles chart record

title: Ethiopians on death row in Saudi Arabia: Prisoners calling the BBC from their cells
description: There was desperation in the voice of the young Ethiopian man when he managed to get through to the BBC from a phone in his prison cell on death row i
body: There was desperation in the voice of the young Ethiopian man when he managed to get through to the BBC from a phone in his prison cell on death row in Saudi Arabia.Habtom, whose name - like the other prisoner featured in this article - has been changed to protect his identity, has been held in a jail in the southern city of Khamis Mushait for more than three years.Above the noise of cellmates shouting behind him, he pleaded for help and sounded angry that his government appeared to be doing little to change his fate."One prisoner cannot comfort another. We have no choice but to cry. We are waiting for our turn, even though we do not know when it will happen," said Habtom.He and some of his fellow inmates had fled war and poverty at home in the hope of finding a better life.But that quest, which took him through Djibouti and Yemen, led to his incarceration - joining a growing number of Ethiopians in Saudi prisons who face the prospect of execution for drug-smuggling offences.Anxious to tell their story, some of the prisoners managed to get hold of the mobile phone number for the BBC's Tigrinya language service. In total we have spoken to seven of the dozens - perhaps as many as 200 - Ethiopians inside the prison who are waiting for a death sentence to be carried out.Other foreigners, including Pakistanis, Sudanese and Jordanians, are in a similar position, but in the first seven months of this year 17 Ethiopians have been executed - the highest number among non-Saudis. Five of those executions happened on Monday.Two years ago, according to research by Amnesty International, just two Ethiopians were executed, but 35 were put to death in 2025.It is not clear exactly why there has been an uptick, but it could be linked to more people leaving the northern Ethiopian region of Tigray, where a brutal two-year civil war in Tigray ended in late 2022, leaving devastation in its wake."It may also be linked to Saudi Arabia's expanding use of the death penalty for drug-related offences in recent years," Amnesty International researcher Dana Ahmed tells the BBC.Habtom, who like most of the those the BBC spoke to is from Tigray, was found guilty of smuggling hashish, a type of cannabis. In Saudi Arabia, on the judge's discretion, a guilty verdict can result in a death sentence.But rights groups - including Reprieve, Human Rights Watch (HRW) and Amnesty International - have said that in these kinds of cases due process is rarely followed.Defendants are not given access to a lawyer or the court papers - while translation, when it is offered, can be inadequate, Amnesty's Ahmed says.Although there is the theoretical right to appeal, without a lawyer they cannot submit one "and then the sentence is automatically upheld", she says."There is a near-total lack of transparency throughout the entire judicial process, from sentencing to Supreme Court review and ratification by the King. People on death row and their families are left in the dark about their fate."Habtom alleged that he was not given the chance to speak to a lawyer or defend himself. He also said he was forced to sign a document in Arabic, which said he agreed to the sentence, without understanding what he was putting his name to.Other prisoners that the BBC spoke to had similar stories about the legal system.HRW has also contacted people close to the cases and learned about "mass sentences, mass trials that lacked any kind of due process and people detained then just waiting with no idea when the sentence would happen", Nadia Hardman, the organisation's senior adviser on refugee and migrant rights, said.The Saudi authorities did not respond to a BBC request for comment on allegations that the legal process was not fair, but every execution is accompanied by a statement issued through the official press agency. It outlines a clear process: an investigation, a court case, an appeal, a Supreme Court ruling and then a royal decree.The sentence reflects the commitment to protect citizens "from the scourge of drugs" and the damage they can cause, the statement adds.Habtom said that although he manged to keep in occasional contact with his family via the wall-mounted phone in his prison cell, he refused to tell them he was on death row: "I would rather they be told after I die than now."He had dreamt of finishing high school, graduating from college and getting a job to support his parents - but the Tigray war put paid to that."My goal was destroyed, so I decided to emigrate," he said.After surviving the dangerous journey to Saudi Arabia in 2021, Habtom found low-paid work as a goatherder, but his employers offered him and others a chance to earn more money.They were asked to deliver a package but were stopped by police on the way and were found with the narcotic leaf known as khat - a natural stimulant that is widely used in the Horn of Africa.The official Saudi statements all refer to hashish smuggling but those the BBC spoke to talked about khat."I did not know what we were carrying. But later I was told it was khat. I don't even know what khat is," Habtom said, admitting that he was tempted into the work by the sum of money on offer.Habtom acknowledged he had "made a mistake without knowing it" and hoped that his sentence could be commuted to prison time.Three of his fellow Ethiopian detainees were executed in April - another nine were killed in June. The April killings sparked an outcry from rights groups and some leading Ethiopian figures, including the influential head of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church.Patriarch Abune Mathias urged the government to negotiate with the Saudi authorities and called the inmates "voiceless children" living "under the shadow of death".In its April report, HRW called on the Saudi authorities to immediately halt executions of Ethiopian migrants and ensure all cases were handled in line with international law. It also asked Ethiopia's foreign ministry to intervene urgently and provide consular support.The safety of Ethiopians in general in Saudi Arabia was raised at a meeting in Addis Ababa in May between Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos and Saudi Deputy Foreign Minister Waleed Al-Khuraiji.This was followed in June by a visit to the prison by Ethiopia's Ambassador Tafa Tulu Dadi, though the prisoners told the BBC that they were not given enough time to explain their situation to him.It also appeared to have limited impact as in the following week more Ethiopians were executed.The African Union's human rights commission has also urged Ethiopia to safeguard the lives of Ethiopians facing execution in Saudi Arabia.The BBC has contacted Ethiopian officials in Saudi Arabia and the government in Addis Ababa for comment but has not received a response.Without referring to the death penalty specifically, Ethiopia's foreign ministry did release a statement on 13 July saying it was in regular contact with the Saudi authorities "pursuing appropriate remedies for Ethiopian citizens facing difficult circumstances".It added that "to date" nearly 2,000 Ethiopians had "benefited from royal amnesties" - without mentioning the crimes or sentences.As they await the outcome of diplomatic manoeuvres, the prisoners who spoke to the BBC said they were enduring hardships in overcrowded facilities.Desta, located in another part of the prison, said there were 200 men in his cell crammed into an area designed for 90 people, with 45 bunk beds arranged around the walls.During the day, the prisoners sat on the floor in stifling conditions squeezed up next to one another; when the temperature dropped at night, they covered themselves with rubbish bags in lieu of bed sheets, he said."The stress of facing execution, combined with the overcrowded conditions, exposes us to illness and anxiety," Desta said."The guard only opens the door to bring food, covering his mouth and nose with a mask - that is the only time the door is opened. After he gives us the food, he quickly locks it and leaves."It is not possible to ask them any questions or speak to them. Even if you ask, there is severe beating."He was arrested while trying to cross the border from Yemen more than three years ago and accused of smuggling drugs."We were four Ethiopians, and there was one Yemeni with us. He told us he could help us cross the border safely because he knew the safest route. In return, he asked us to carry packages containing khat and even promised to pay us some money."Unfortunately, shortly after we crossed, we were captured by police officers. They opened fire on us, and the Yemeni man ran away, but we couldn't. We were shocked and had no idea where to go."Like all those interviewed by the BBC, Desta said he had never expected to be sentenced to death and believed he would eventually return home after serving time in prison.Instead, he alleged that he was also forced to sign a document in Arabic that listed charges carrying capital punishment. Later, when he appeared in court, he said that he was denied the chance to challenge the charges and had no legal representation."When you appear before the judge on the first day, he asks: 'Do you accept the charges?' On the second appearance, he sentences you to death," Desta said.As a brick-maker struggling to support his family, he had left Tigray during the war as the fighting edged closer to his home.Now he worries for his life again - and he, Habtom and dozens of others on death row are begging for outside help."We are living in deep fear and cannot even eat the food we are given," said Habtom.Additional reporting by Damian Zane

schema.headline: Ethiopians on death row in Saudi Arabia: Prisoners calling the BBC from their cells

title: Will Fifa president Gianni Infantino lose his job? If so, who comes in?
description: Life moves fast for Fifa president Gianni Infantino.It was doing so earlier this month as he was zig-zagging across the United States in a private jet
body: Life moves fast for Fifa president Gianni Infantino.It was doing so earlier this month as he was zig-zagging across the United States in a private jet to make him virtually omnipresent as the World Cup reached its crescendo.On 19 July he must have felt on top of the world as, together with US President Donald Trump, they handed the trophy over to Spain.Less than two weeks later, Infantino is in a lonely place after scrapping controversial plans to sell off stakes in Fifa competitions to private investment.Condemned by UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, castigated by fans of the game he professes to want to protect. These can easily be deflected as hazards of the job.Less so the threatened boycott of Fifa competitions by European governing body Uefa - an attack reinforced by Concacaf (North and Central America and the Caribbean) and the AFC (Asia).All three organisations, in their own way, offered a withering assessment of how Fifa is being run under Infantino."This issue extends far beyond a single proposal," said the AFC. "Rather, it has exposed fundamental weaknesses in Fifa's consultation and decision-making processes that must now be addressed."Sources say, in addition to rejecting Infantino's plan, the vast majority of the Concacaf members are either losing faith in the Fifa president's ability to govern the game, or have lost it altogether.On top of that, Carlos Cordeiro, special advisor to Infantino and appointed by Trump as senior advisor to the White House Task Force on the 2026 World Cup, has resigned.Fifa's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said in a statement to Associated Press that Fifa's own administration was "deceived" about the project.BBC Sport has approached Fifa for comment.It feels as though the walls are closing in on Infantino.But if this is the beginning of the end of his tenure, who takes over?Firstly, it is wise to be realistic.Speaking to BBC Sport earlier this week, former Football Association chairman David Bernstein said of Infantino: "In a normal organisation, if he has to back down due to something of this magnitude he'd probably be shown the door."But Fifa is not a normal organisation. If he has the support of enough of the national associations, he will continue."Former Fifa vice-president Jim Boyce said he thinks Infantino will "still have enough support" to be re-elected but "if things continue at the pace they are continuing, who knows?"He added: "If I was a betting man, which I'm not, I would still bet he will get his final four-year term."Infantino has been Fifa president since 2016. Before that he was secretary general of Uefa for seven years. Few know the map of football politics better than him.Now 56, Infantino became president by beating Asian Football Confederation president Sheikh Salman al-Khalifa by 115 votes to 88. His task was to clean up an organisation tainted by corruption allegations following the resignation of predecessor Sepp Blatter. Blatter was cleared of corruption charges last year."I will work tirelessly to bring football back to Fifa and Fifa back to football," said Infantino at the time.Infantino has twice been re-elected unopposed, and it was expected the same thing would happen again next March. This is not unusual. Blatter was unopposed in 2007 and 2011.Brazilian Joao Havelange was the last person to unseat a Fifa president in an election, ousting Sir Stanley Rous in 1974. No-one opposed Havelange for five straight terms until he finally resigned in 1998, aged 82.Letters of support backing Infantino's re-election have been submitted. Will they be withdrawn? BBC Sport knows of at least one Uefa member who has withdrawn their letter as the drama of this week has unfolded.Victor Montagliani (Concacaf president)Like Infantino, he was elected in 2016 promising governance reform. A former president of Canada Soccer, as co-chair, Montagliani was heavily involved in the build up to, and delivery of the 2026 World Cup, the first to be hosted by three nations. He is fluent in French, Italian and Spanish, as well as English.Explaining his decision to run for the Concacaf presidency, Montagliani told the BC Business website: "Like anything, when I decide to go, I go. I campaigned on my own dime for three months, went to see all 41 countries, from the US to Bonaire, a little island off Venezuela."Montagliani took the lead when Concacaf hosted an expanded Copa America in 2024 - in an interview with BBC Sport he rejected the idea it could become a regular occurrence. Politically strong, he smoothed relations around Arsene Wenger's attempt to gain support for a World Cup every two years and has never truly bought into the idea of a 64-team World Cup.At the Leaders conference in 2025, he outlined why he felt football was strong enough to ride out any storm."The game is bigger than world current leaders," he said. "Football will survive regimes. Does it cause a headache? Of course. You have to be realistic about that. That is the beauty of our game, it is bigger than any individual and country."Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa (AFC president)Initially elected in 2013, he was elected unopposed for a fourth term to run to 2027.The Bahraini has presided over significant growth within the Asian confederation, through the Champions League Elite, Champions League Two, the Challenge League and the Women's Champions League, which was launched in 2024-25. The Asian Cup has been expanded to 24 teams.Sheikh Salman signed off the brutal takedown of how Fifa is being run by Infantino and has carried with him a 46-member confederation, many of whom are aware the figures being offered by Infantino's plan are huge in terms of their overall football expenditure.Nasser Al-Khelaifi (PSG president and chair of European Football Clubs - EFC)Previously known as the European Clubs' Association, Al-Khelaifi took over as chairman in the aftermath of the other seismic event that threatened to pull the game apart - the ill-fated European Super League, which collapsed within 48 hours in 2021.Al-Khelaifi presided over a name change - to European Football Clubs. More importantly, he expanded it to more than 800 members. Of the biggest clubs, only Real Madrid remain outside.In theory, the Qatari would be a serious challenger to Infantino. But it seems he doesn't want the role. "He genuinely, genuinely, genuinely doesn't want the job," was the response of a source close to the 52-year-old when asked about the possibility on Thursday.Mattias Grafstrom (Fifa secretary general)Appointed in May 2024 and an increasingly influential voice around the Fifa table.Multi-lingual, Grafstrom become Infantino's chief of staff following his election as president in 2016.Another very visual presence at the World Cup, he could be seen as being too close to Infantino - and the general feeling Fifa's next president needs to be a non-European might also count against him.Fifa's next president will be confirmed at the organisation's 77th Congress in Morocco next March. Candidates have until 18 November to put their names forward.

schema.headline: Will Fifa president Gianni Infantino lose his job? If so, who comes in?

title: Victims of Robert Bush call for funeral industry regulation
description: Victims of disgraced funeral boss demand industry regulationImage source, PAImage caption, Relatives of the victims of Robert Bush call for funeral in
body: Victims of disgraced funeral boss demand industry regulationImage source, PAImage caption, Relatives of the victims of Robert Bush call for funeral industry regulation outside his sentencing hearing at Hull Crown CourtByPaul Murphyin Hull and Paul JohnsonEast Yorkshire and LincolnshireTristan Essex is standing on the steps of Hull Crown Court, shoulder to shoulder with several others whose lives have been devastated by disgraced funeral director Robert Bush. The 27-year-old is fighting alongside his sister Claire for regulation of the funeral industry, a journey that has seen them take their campaign to Downing Street and resulted in a new pledge from the government "to take urgent action to crack down on rogue funeral operators".Their grandmother Jessie Stockdale was one of Bush's victims – her body one of the 35 found at Legacy Independent Funeral Directors, five months after her funeral was held.The news knocked the family off its feet, Tristan said. Even worse, they learned the ashes they had been given were not Jessie's remains.This story contains details some might find distressing.Image source, Tristan EssexImage caption, Tristan Essex says his memories of his nana, Jessie Stockdale, are "tainted" after Bush kept her body for five months after her funeralOn Friday, Bush was jailed for 20 years for a litany of crimes. He failed to bury or cremate people, gave bereaved relatives the ashes of strangers and defrauded nearly 200 families out of more than £500,000.It is nearly two years since Tristan and Claire launched their campaign. Outside court, the group's small white posters were printed with a QR code that linked to a parliamentary petition for "full statutory regulation" of the funeral industry. "You can start your own funeral directors from your shed," said Tristan. "No regulations, no laws, no qualifications. The government's had forever to do it and we're still waiting."Police fear further victims in funeral home horrorMoment police officers set foot in 'horror scene' funeral homeFollowing sentencing, the Department for Health and Social Care said it would develop "proposals for formal regulation of the funeral sector", with families due to be consulted.Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, said: "In the wake of this horrific case, we will now bring forward comprehensive proposals to ensure respect and dignity for the deceased in every setting, including proper regulation of the funeral sector."Prime Minister Andy Burnham also backed regulation and said he wanted to ensure "the highest standards" applied.Image source, Humberside PoliceImage caption, Bush himself highlighted the lack of industry regulation during police interviewsThe funeral industry in England, Wales and Northern Ireland is self-regulating, relying on voluntary codes and inspections by trade associations. Anyone can set up as a funeral director without formal training, registration or mandatory oversight.Bush himself highlighted the lack of regulation during his interviews with Humberside Police.In footage released by the force, an officer asks: "Has it ever happened in your experience that someone from Bereavement Services, for example, has turned up to ask to inspect your fridges to make sure they are in order?"Bush replies: "No, nobody."The officer asks: "Is [inspection] a thing that happens?""When you join the National Association of Funeral Directors (NAFD) you have an inspection," Bush responds."They came round for spot inspections, but if you didn't come up to scratch there wasn't a penalty, you just weren't in their association any more."Bush shrugs."They're also checking whether you've got cushions on your sofa or how many leaflets you have."He later adds: "I know we're a highly unregulated industry."Image source, Humberside PoliceImage caption, Police photographed scenes of chaos at Bush's business in Hessle Road, HullBush admitted 67 offences, including 30 counts of preventing a lawful and decent burial.The NAFD previously told the BBC how Legacy resigned its membership of its organisation in 2021.In a statement, its CEO Andrew Judd described Bush's crimes as "deeply shocking" and said families in Hull had been let down by "his unspeakable actions."Addressing calls for regulation, he added: "Our position at the NAFD has always been clear – we want to see independent statutory regulation of all funeral directors."That need was illustrated by the chaos and neglect captured in images and body-worn camera footage taken by police at Legacy.The inside of the Hessle Road premises was described in court as resembling a "horror scene".Image caption, Judge Mr Justice Hilliard has called for an explanation about the absence of forms used to monitor burial or cremation in the Bush caseThe question remains why Bush's abuse of the system was not spotted by those he needed to regularly work with to conduct cremations and burials.His sentencing hearing was told forms used to monitor and record burials and cremations had not been returned and, according to the prosecution, "not followed up by the assigned registrar".Judge Mr Justice Hilliard asked in court: "Why didn't they? What's the explanation? There's public interest in this. They want to know what's happened."Prosecution barrister Steven Ball later read out a joint statement from Hull City Council and East Riding of Yorkshire Council, in which the authorities said registrars were meant to inform the national general register office about missing certificates, but "that did not happen".However, the councils added: "Because the process as a whole doesn't provide the necessary oversight, it is not clear whether this would have changed the outcome of this tragic case."The authorities said the current framework for the funeral sector relied heavily on trust and called "for reform and registration".Sentencing Bush on Friday, the judge said "there were no checks over many years of the way in which he conducted his business" and "no oversight" of the condition in which the deceased were kept."A single visit might have been enough to bring some of what he was doing to a halt," he added.Image caption, Nigel Hotham with his sister ZoeNigel Hotham's uncle, Mark Hotham, died in September 2023. His body was later found in Bush's funeral parlour. Speaking after the hearing, Nigel said it was "about time" the government acted and he was glad Burnham was listening."It's important that he does," he said. "Things do need to change and they need to change fast."It's easier to open a funeral director's than it is to open a sandwich shop – and there's more regulation around sandwich shops than there is funeral directors."We're campaigning massively for change."Image caption, Karen Dry used Legacy to cremate the bodies of both of her parents Karen Dry, who fears the ashes given to her by Legacy did not belong to her parents, Allan and Betty, said only a "full public inquiry" would satisfy her."There is an enduring sense of deep betrayal, emotional stress and damage caused by this individual to many families right across this city," she said.Speaking after Bush was jailed, she added: "Without this regulation, I can guarantee you one thing: in five or 10 years time there will be another funeral director with another 300 families in a courtroom somewhere else getting another 20 years for doing exactly this. "We've got to put a stop to it and it's got to stop now."Image source, PAImage caption, Police discovered 35 bodies and more than 100 sets of ashes when they raided the premises in March 2024Concerns about the treatment of the dead in both mortuary and funeral home settings did not begin with the Robert Bush case.Disturbing cases of neglect and malpractice in Gosport and Leeds have previously prompted calls for regulation. Meanwhile, the 2021 inquiry into the abuse by David Fuller at the mortuary of Maidstone and Tunbridge Wells NHS Trust concluded the funeral sector was, in effect, "an unregulated free-for-all".It recommended, external the government establish an independent statutory regulatory scheme for funeral directors in England "as a matter of urgency".In Friday's statement, the government referred to the Fuller inquiry, but made no mention of a statutory scheme. Image caption, Kevin Moxon, another funeral director in Hull, said Bush's actions had harmed the industryKevin Moxon, who runs Moxon's Family Funeral Directors in Hull's Anlaby Road, said he was concerned "trust in our industry" had been badly damaged."This case [Robert Bush] is not indicative of how our profession runs. It's a sacred duty to look after someone's loved one," he said."We need regulation bringing in pretty rapidly. We need inspectors coming round doing spot checks to ensure that we are all running to a set code of practice."Following the government's announcement, Judd said the NAFD would make the case for statutory regulation as the best way to secure "meaningful change". He told the BBC:  "Our call for reform is about safeguarding the deceased and the bereaved. The dead cannot protect themselves. "That responsibility falls to the rest of us."Watch the story of Robert Bush and Legacy funeral directors in a new programme on BBC iPlayer.If you have been affected by issues surrounding bereavement, information is available via BBC Action Line, including contact details of organisations that can help.Get in touchYour Voice

schema.headline: Victims of Robert Bush call for funeral industry regulation

title: Bev Craig: Who is the new Mayor of Greater Manchester?
description: Image source, Labour PartyImage caption, Bev Craig has been elected as the new mayor of Greater ManchesterByLauren HirstNorth West and Kevin Fitzpatri
body: Image source, Labour PartyImage caption, Bev Craig has been elected as the new mayor of Greater ManchesterByLauren HirstNorth West and Kevin FitzpatrickBBC Manchester political reporterBev Craig will succeed UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham as Greater Manchester's mayor after winning Thursday's by-election.The Labour candidate claimed victory after securing 309,525 votes over Reform's Sian Astley who won 157,178.Burnham stood down after winning the Makerfield by-election in June to return to the House of Commons. He subsequently became prime minister on 20 June.But who is Bev Craig, what has she done, and what does she stand for? Will she closely follow her predecessor's agenda or does she have different priorities for a city region which consists of 10 boroughs and is home to more than two million people?Having grown up on a council estate in Belfast, Craig moved to Manchester in 2003 at the age of 18 to study politics and modern history at the University of Manchester.After graduating, she began her career in local government. She went on to work in higher education and then at a national trade union, leading on social care.Craig was first elected as a councillor for the Burnage ward on Manchester City Council in 2011.She was executive member for adult social care and health throughout the Covid-19 global pandemic, before becoming deputy council leader in 2021.Craig soon took over as leader when Sir Richard Leese stood down after 25 years in the role.Her promotion made her the local authority's first female boss and the council's first openly gay leader.The 41-year-old has also held the role of deputy mayor for economy, business and inclusive growth on the Greater Manchester Combined Authority.She was awarded the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in the New Year Honours List in 2025 for services to local government.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Craig, pictured with her partner Tracy, on polling day on Thursday Key achievements and challengesAs council leader, Craig has overseen sustained annual economic growth in Manchester of more than 3% during the last decade, making it one of the fastest growing city economies in Europe.The main criticism since Craig became council leader has been around the lack of affordable housing at a time when skyscrapers have been built in the city centre. Although, in her tenure the local authority has built social housing for the first time in 40 years.In November 2025, children's services in Manchester were rated as "outstanding" by inspectors after a decade-long process of improvement. The service had been rated "inadequate" by Ofsted in 2014 and it was not until 2022 that it was deemed to be "good".However, an issue that has brought negative headlines during Craig's career has been crime and anti-social behaviour, notably in the city centre's flagship communal area of Piccadilly Gardens. The latest in a long line of multi-million pound plans to revamp it was launched in February 2026 and work is under way to make it "an attractive world-class space". Despite a high-profile policing operation, regular incidents of violence still occur there.Image caption, Bev Craig became leader of Manchester City Council five years agoWhat has she promised?After she was announced as Labour's candidate to succeed Westminster-bound Burnham, Craig said she was ready to "deliver the next chapter for the region".Her headline campaign pledges have been to freeze Metrolink and bus fares on the Bee Network and extend free bus travel to 11 to 18-year-olds. Currently, only 16 to 18-year-olds benefit from the scheme.She said: "I will work every day for us to make sure everyone shares in the success Greater Manchester is building - making sure there's more money in people's pockets, pride in every town centre with a New High Streets Fund, a new generation of council and affordable homes, and an expanded Bee Network that freezes fares and that works for all of us."She said she was committed to delivering 50,000 new homes in a mix of council properties and genuinely affordable housing over the next 15 years. Craig said she would also launch a new £20m high street scheme, promising it would support small businesses, revitalise empty units and invest in town-centre regeneration.Labour Party's Bev Craig's mayoral candidate interviewBBC Radio Manchester interviewed each candidate in the mayoral by-election.

schema.headline: Bev Craig: Who is the new Mayor of Greater Manchester?

title: FLO say they 'want it all' after new album Therapy at the Club
description: British girl band FLO 'want it all' - and they're confident they will get itImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, FLO won Best R&B/Soul Act at the
body: British girl band FLO 'want it all' - and they're confident they will get itImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, FLO won Best R&B/Soul Act at the 2026 MOBO Awards and received their first Grammy nomination this yearByLola Schroer"It's kind of been like a bit of a crash course in making music," says Stella Quaresma of making FLO's second album, Therapy at the Club.After entering the music industry as teenagers, the British girl band say they grew to trust their own instincts during six months making their new record.Formed of Quaresma, Jorja Douglas and Renée Downer, they first broke through in 2022 with the track Cardboard Box and have since won Best R&B/Soul Act at the 2026 MOBO Awards.The group have more than five million monthly Spotify listeners, 1.2 million TikTok followers and almost 58 million likes on the platform. The campaign around their second album has included a NPR Tiny Desk performance viewed over a million times and appearances on high-profile US podcasts, helping reintroduce them stateside."It felt like we went to university and graduated with honours," Quaresma adds.For their latest album, the group say they became more involved than ever before in every stage of the album's creation, from songwriting and vocal arrangements to production decisions.'We're definitely a lot more grown up'"Sometimes you walk away from a session and people are surprised that you contributed, that you had ideas," says Douglas. Quaresma suggests that's partly because when FLO first entered the industry, they leaned on the experience of the writers and producers around them."In the past we'd kind of been okay with that," she says. "But now we really don't need that kind of crutch."For Downer, that greater creative control has resulted in FLO's most authentic record yet."We're definitely a lot more grown up. We've been a lot more involved, so this really is the best reflection of us at this point in time," she says.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, All three knew of one another from social media before forming as a group in 2019Love has always been central to FLO's music, but on this album they explore its messier realities, with nights out providing the backdrop for stories of heartbreak, healing and friendship."So go ahead and kiss who you wanna / whatever the trauma / If you ever fall out of love / try therapy at the club," they sing on the title track.Quaresma says the title came to represent the role friends can play during difficult moments."It's the idea that you're having the worst time of your life, but your friends are saying, 'No, you're coming out, you're going to dance and forget about it for a second.'"While R&B remains at the heart of FLO's sound, they say they also aimed to push further into pop on their second album.Quaresma says making Therapy at the Club taught her "how fun it is to really blend genres and to delve more into making pop music to make really big songs".One example is Remedied, co-written with Grammy-winning songwriter Amy Allen, who has worked with pop stars Sabrina Carpenter and Tate McRae.When making their Grammy-nominated debut album, Access All Areas, the FLO trio wrote songs together - but for Therapy at the Club, they wrote separately before bringing ideas back to one another. Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, FLO's debut album, Access All Areas was nominated for Best Progressive R&B Album at the 2026 Grammys. Quaresma says this process helped them appreciate one another's strengths in a new way."You don't fully get to appreciate each other's talents when you're writing in a room of 10 people. To go away and write songs, then show each other what we'd made, was really special," she says.That approach also extended to the album's collaborations. One of just two guest appearances on the record is Sex in Peace, their second collaboration with rising British R&B singer kwn. Quaresma wrote the song before bringing it to the rest of the group.Downer says working with kwn has become a natural fit. "We work really well with kwn when it comes to sexy R&B, so it felt right to send it to her and see if she'd do a verse," she says."She sent it back really quickly. We had no notes. We loved it."'This is the most thrilling, entertaining, fulfilling job'FLO's ambition doesn't stop with the music. Live performance is never far from their minds, with choreography, visuals and music videos all considered throughout the album-making process. "As we elevate everywhere else in our career, with the vocals, the music, the appearance, we also want to elevate the music videos and the dance," Douglas explains.The demanding schedule has meant long rehearsal days and little sleep, but Douglas says it's worth it."This is the most thrilling, entertaining, fulfilling job we could have ever asked for."Asked what success looks like over the next year, the trio don't hesitate."We want it all," Quaresma says.Douglas nods in agreement before adding: "We want the shows, we want the numbers, we want the awards, we want the love and we want the success."

schema.headline: FLO say they 'want it all' after new album Therapy at the Club

title: CPS to target assets of jailed Legacy funeral director Robert Bush
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Robert Bush sold fake funeral plans and stole from charitiesByLinsey Smith and Kevin ShoesmithEast Yo
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Robert Bush sold fake funeral plans and stole from charitiesByLinsey Smith and Kevin ShoesmithEast Yorkshire and LincolnshireA disgraced funeral director's bank accounts and assets have been frozen, as prosecutors seek to recover cash fleeced from his victims.Robert Bush was jailed for 20 years at Hull Crown Court on Friday for 67 offences, including denying 30 people a decent and proper burial and giving families the ashes of strangers.Bush, 48, who ran Legacy Independent Funeral Directors in Hull, stole up to £12,000 from charities and sold fake funeral plans.Laura Tams KC, deputy chief crown prosecutor at the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), said: "We will be looking at him, at the financial aspects of this case, to see if we can confiscate any of the proceeds of his crimes and try to compensate the families."Sentencing Bush following a five-day hearing, Mr Justice Hilliard said it was clear that he "benefited very substantially" and "obviously lived very well".Speaking exclusively to the BBC, Tams said it "was not a case of somebody that had recently fallen on hard times".She added: "I think the scale of the offending, the length of time it had gone on for, showed that really this had become something of his business model."Image source, Humberside PoliceImage caption, Messy scenes like this met officers who raided Legacy Independent Funeral Directors in March 2024Bush's litany of crimes included leaving the remains of a stillborn baby on the floor for two years and giving the grieving parents the wrong ashes, the court heard.In court, barrister Richard Wright KC said his client, who admitted the charges, was a man of previous good character who had "lost his good name and his livelihood".Wright said "greed, incompetence and an inability to keep up with his own failings" had all played a part in his crimes.In police interviews, Bush – whose funeral parlour was found in a state of chaos when officers raided it – told how debts had accrued, leaving him unable to pay for cremations.Yet in court, it emerged that Bush took £162,000 a year for himself and transferred an average of £52,000 a year to his wife.Several thousand pounds a year were spent on holidays, flights and hotels, records show.Between 2017 and 2024, the total amount of money paid into both Legacy and Bush's personal accounts was more than £3.5m.Image source, Facebook/Robert BushImage caption, Robert Bush enjoyed motorbike racing and often posted on social media about racing his own bikesUntil he moved to an address in Otley, West Yorkshire, as part of his bail conditions, Bush lived in an affluent part of the East Riding of Yorkshire.He enjoyed motorcycle racing and was arrested at Heathrow Airport after a holiday in the United States.   Describing it as a "shocking" case, with "really serious breaches of trust", Tams said more than 13,000 pages of prosecution evidence had been compiled. Families had been misled by Bush since 2012, investigators found.Besides the failure to cremate bodies placed in his care, it became apparent there were "much wider aspects" of Bush's offending, said Tams."He was fraudulently trading in funeral plans when he wasn't authorised to do so, and there was over 200 people that were affected by that."They thought that they were investing in their future funeral care, they thought that he [Bush] would have been investing that money with financial institutions. But, in fact, he had kept that money for his own purposes."Tams said the CPS's priority throughout had been to ensure it built a "robust" case that showed the full extent of Bush's offending "so that the families could get justice". Image source, Humberside PoliceImage caption, Bush is believed to have stolen up to £12,000 from charitiesA total of 12 charities had lost money, the court heard."Families had left donations that they wanted to go to charitable causes on behalf of their loved ones," said Tams. "And on 12 occasions that we know of, that money was not received by the charities."Prosecutors were unable to say exactly how much money Bush had stolen from charity collection boxes over a period of six years and six months, but the court was told they put the figure at between £5,540 and £12,000.Some of the families involved in the case have called for regulation of the funeral industry.Tams said the case had "uncovered really serious and fundamental flaws" in the industry."The fact that his business had been able to run in this way for so many years and left unidentified is deeply troubling," she said.Watch the story of Robert Bush and Legacy funeral directors in a new programme on BBC iPlayer.If you have been affected by issues surrounding bereavement, information is available via BBC Action Line, including contact details of organisations that can help.Get in touchYour Voice
